title: THEY WERE ALREADY DIVIDING THE WOMEN—BUT GOD HAD ALREADY DECIDED THE BATTLE
paragraphs: THEY WERE ALREADY DIVIDING THE WOMEN—BUT GOD HAD ALREADY DECIDED THE BATTLE
The Terrifying Words Hidden in Deborah’s Song: How Judges 5 Exposes the Cruelty of War, the Arrogance of Powerful Men, and the God Who Hears Those the World Treats as Spoils
Somewhere, a mother was waiting for her son to come home from war. She did not know that the victory she imagined would have meant another mother's daughter never coming home at all.
Read that again.
Because buried inside one of the oldest victory songs in Scripture is a moment so disturbing that many Christians have read past it without realizing what they were hearing.
A woman is standing at a window.
She is looking down the road.
She is waiting for the sound of chariots.
Her son is a powerful military commander. He has hundreds of iron chariots under his command. He has gone to war against people his kingdom has oppressed for twenty years.
Surely, he will return victorious.
Surely, there will be treasures.
Surely, there will be celebrations.
But the chariots do not come.
And as his mother begins to wonder why, the women around her offer an explanation that reveals something horrifying about the world they inhabit.
Perhaps the soldiers are taking their time dividing the spoils.
Perhaps they are collecting the treasures.
Perhaps each warrior is choosing a woman.
Or two.
Not wives waiting to be courted.
Not women being asked for consent.
Captives.
Human beings being counted among the rewards of conquest.
And the most chilling part?
The women speaking about them appear to regard this as an ordinary expectation of military victory.
This is not a scene from a modern war documentary.
This is the Bible.
Judges chapter 5.
And once you understand what Deborah is singing, you may never read this passage the same way again.
Because the Song of Deborah does something extraordinary.
It allows the enemy's own imagined expectations to expose the moral ugliness of his world.
And then it leaves us with a question that reaches far beyond the ancient battlefield.
What happens when human beings become so accustomed to cruelty that they stop recognizing it as cruelty?
The story begins long before that mother looks through her window.
Israel has again turned away from the LORD.
Judges 4:1 tells us that after Ehud died, the Israelites once more did evil in the sight of God.
The consequences were devastating.
Jabin, king of Canaan, ruled from Hazor, and Sisera commanded his army.
Sisera possessed nine hundred iron chariots.
For an ancient population without comparable military strength, that was a terrifying advantage.
Imagine hearing those wheels approaching.
Imagine knowing that the soldiers coming toward your village have weapons you cannot match.
Imagine wondering whether your children will survive the day.
Judges 4:3 says Sisera oppressed the Israelites harshly for twenty years.
Twenty years.
Long enough for a frightened child to become an anxious parent.
Long enough for an entire generation to grow up thinking oppression was normal.
Long enough for people to begin believing that the powerful would always remain powerful.
But the text says something that changes everything.
The children of Israel cried out to the LORD.
And God heard.
Not because Israel had earned deliverance.
Not because their record of obedience was impressive.
Not because they had suddenly become strong enough to defeat their enemies.
They cried out because they were desperate.
And the God of Israel was not deaf to their suffering.
There is someone reading this who understands that kind of desperation.
You have prayed until the words stopped coming.
You have endured something for so long that you no longer remember what peace feels like.
You have watched people with power make decisions that wounded people without power.
And perhaps, somewhere in the exhaustion, you have wondered whether God notices.
Judges 4 and 5 do not promise that every hardship will end immediately.
But they testify that oppression does not escape God's attention.
And that human power is never ultimate.
Into this story steps Deborah.
A prophetess.
A judge in Israel.
A woman through whom God speaks at a time when the nation desperately needs courage and direction.
She summons Barak and communicates the LORD's command to gather ten thousand men from Naphtali and Zebulun.
God promises to draw Sisera toward the Kishon River and give him into Barak's hand.
Barak hesitates.
He tells Deborah that he will go if she goes with him.
Deborah agrees, but announces that the honor of defeating Sisera will go to a woman.
The reader might naturally assume that woman will be Deborah.
But Scripture has another surprise waiting.
When the battle comes, Sisera's military advantage collapses.
Judges 4:15 describes the LORD throwing Sisera and his chariots into confusion before Barak.
Judges 5 later celebrates the battle in vivid poetic language, including the intervention of the stars and the Kishon River.
The song presents the victory as the LORD's work, not merely the triumph of Israelite military strategy.
Sisera abandons his chariot.
The commander who once inspired terror is now running on foot.
He reaches the tent of Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite.
Jael welcomes him inside.
She covers him.
He asks for water.
She gives him milk.
He asks her to stand guard and conceal his presence.
Then, while he sleeps, she takes a tent peg and a hammer and kills him.
The account is violent.
Scripture does not soften it.
Judges 5 praises Jael for her decisive role in Sisera's defeat, while Judges 4 recounts the event with stark narrative detail.
We should neither pretend the violence is absent nor turn it into entertainment.
This is a story emerging from a brutal ancient world, where the survival of communities could be bound up with the defeat of oppressive armies.
And then Deborah sings.
Her song is not a detached historical report.
It is poetry.
It is worship.
It is a celebration of deliverance.
It remembers courage, hesitation, suffering, and divine intervention.
And near the end, it turns our attention away from the battlefield.
Away from Barak.
Away from Deborah.
Away from Jael.
And into the home of the defeated commander.
There, at the window, is Sisera's mother.
Judges 5:28 says in the King James Version:
"The mother of Sisera looked out at a window, and cried through the lattice, Why is his chariot so long in coming? why tarry the wheels of his chariots?"
The scene is almost painfully human.
A mother waiting.
A road remaining empty.
An unanswered question.
But the emotional force of the passage is not simply that an enemy commander has a mother who misses him.
It is what the people around her assume he is doing.
Judges 5:30 gives their imagined explanation:
"Have they not sped? have they not divided the prey; to every man a damsel or two; to Sisera a prey of divers colours..."
Pause there.
"To every man a damsel or two."
Those English words can sound almost harmless to modern ears.
But the Hebrew is far more unsettling.
The Masoretic Hebrew text includes the expression:
רַחַם רַחֲמָתַיִם לְרֹאשׁ גֶּבֶר
Raḥam raḥămātayim le-rosh gever.
A close rendering of the phrase is:
"A womb, two wombs, for each man."
That is not the smooth language most modern readers expect from a Bible translation.
And it is precisely why the original wording deserves careful attention.
The Hebrew noun raḥam is associated with the womb. Here, in the context of distributing war spoils, it is used to refer to female captives in a profoundly objectifying way.
The expression is not a tender celebration of motherhood.
It reduces women to their reproductive anatomy while treating them as portions of plunder.
Many English translations communicate the referent rather than reproducing the anatomical wording.
The ESV renders the relevant phrase as "A womb or two for every man," while other translations use language such as "a girl or two" or "a woman or two."
Those differences matter.
The translations are attempting to communicate a difficult ancient expression, but the literal imagery makes the dehumanization especially difficult to ignore.
In the enemy's imagined celebration, captive women are being counted.
Allocated.
Distributed.
The text does not narrate these particular assaults as completed events. The women at Sisera's home are imagining the victorious army dividing its spoils.
That distinction is important.
Deborah is exposing what Sisera's household expects from victory, not reporting that Sisera successfully captured these women in this battle.
And what they expect is horrifying.
The passage strongly evokes the sexual exploitation of female war captives, a known danger in ancient warfare.
The women are placed in the same catalogue of anticipated rewards as decorated garments and embroidered cloth.
People alongside property.
Human bodies alongside possessions.
And the song's dramatic irony is devastating.
While Sisera's mother imagines her son receiving the spoils of victory, the audience already knows he is dead.
The man expected to return as a conqueror has been defeated.
The army expected to divide captives has been scattered.
The iron chariots expected to crush the oppressed have failed.
And the woman waiting at the window does not yet understand what has happened.
There is something deeply uncomfortable about that scene.
We can recognize a mother's anxiety while refusing to excuse the cruelty reflected in her expectations.
We can acknowledge the humanity of an enemy's family without forgetting the humanity of the women they expected to enslave.
And perhaps that is part of what makes this ancient poem so piercing.
It forces us to see how ordinary affection and moral blindness can exist in the same human heart.
A person can love someone deeply and still accept terrible things that person does to others.
A community can celebrate its heroes while ignoring its victims.
A culture can become so accustomed to injustice that its people discuss suffering as though it were an ordinary benefit of success.
And before we condemn an ancient household too quickly, we should ask whether we recognize any of that in ourselves.
How easily do we overlook suffering when it benefits our side?
How often do we defend people we admire without listening to those they have harmed?
How many times have we treated someone's pain as less important because acknowledging it would disturb our comfort?
It is easy to recognize cruelty when the villain belongs to another generation.
It is harder to recognize our own compromises.
And this is where Scripture stops being a distant account of ancient warfare and begins examining the reader.
Not because every person is guilty of the same atrocities.
But because every human heart needs God's truth to expose the places where love has grown selective and conscience has become quiet.
We should also be careful about what the Song of Deborah does and does not teach.
Judges 5 is a victory hymn celebrating the LORD's deliverance of Israel from an oppressive military power.
It is not a comprehensive Christian treatise on war.
It does not mean that every act of violence described in the book of Judges is a universal moral instruction for believers.
It does not authorize Christians to mistreat enemies, celebrate sexual violence, or use divine judgment as an excuse for personal cruelty.
The book of Judges repeatedly portrays a deeply troubled world, and the distinction between what Scripture describes and what God commands remains essential.
The poetry of Judges 5 is powerful precisely because it does not allow the enemy's expectation of captive women to disappear beneath the language of military glory.
It brings that expectation into view.
And then it reverses the anticipated outcome.
Sisera's mother waits for a victory that will never arrive.
The oppressed have been delivered.
The conqueror has fallen.
But there is an even deeper question for Christians reading this passage.
Where does this story lead us when we read the whole Bible through the revelation of Jesus Christ?
Because Deborah's song exposes a world in which power is used to dominate.
And the Gospel reveals a King whose greatness is displayed through sacrificial love.
Consider the difference.
Sisera's household imagines victory as taking.
Taking treasure.
Taking garments.
Taking women.
Taking whatever the defeated cannot protect.
But Jesus describes His mission in radically different terms.
Mark 10:45 says:
"For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many."
Read that slowly.
The Son of Man did not come to seize human beings as the spoils of His power.
He came to give His own life.
He did not come to exploit the vulnerable.
He came to serve.
He did not conquer by making innocent people bear the cost of His selfish ambition.
He willingly bore suffering to accomplish redemption.
This does not erase the historical meaning of Judges 5 or turn Deborah's song into a hidden prediction of Jesus.
The original song concerns Israel's deliverance from Sisera.
But when Christians read it within the larger biblical story, its portrait of abusive human power stands in striking contrast to the character and mission of Christ.
And that contrast matters.
Because Jesus shows us what righteous kingship looks like.
The world says power means having the right to take.
Jesus shows that true greatness is expressed in humble service.
The world often measures victory by how many people submit to the conqueror.
Jesus lays down His life to redeem sinners.
The world may treat vulnerable people as expendable.
Jesus receives people whom others overlook, dishonor, and reject.
Think about the woman brought before Jesus in John 8.
She stands publicly accused.
Others are ready to use her shame as the occasion for condemnation.
But Jesus refuses to let the crowd turn her into an object for its purposes.
He exposes the hypocrisy of her accusers.
He does not declare sin harmless.
He tells her to leave her life of sin.
Yet He refuses to reduce her entire identity to the accusation surrounding her.
"Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more."
John 8:11.
That is not permission to remain unchanged.
It is mercy that calls a person toward a different life.
And there is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Jesus does not save us by pretending sin is insignificant.
He saves sinners through His death and resurrection, calling us to repentance and faith.
Grace is not the denial of evil.
Grace is God's undeserved favor reaching people who cannot rescue themselves.
Forgiveness is not a declaration that wounds do not matter.
It is made possible through the costly work of Christ.
And transformation is not merely learning to appear religious.
It is the work of God changing our hearts, our loyalties, and the way we treat other people.
Perhaps you have been treated like something to be used.
Perhaps someone valued what you could provide but never cared about what you were carrying.
Perhaps your trust was exploited.
Your dignity was disregarded.
Your suffering was minimized.
And somewhere along the way, you began to wonder whether your worth had been permanently damaged by what happened to you.
Hear this carefully.
What another person did to you does not determine the worth God gave you.
You were made in the image of God.
Genesis 1:27 grounds human dignity in the Creator Himself.
Your humanity is not something an abuser, an oppressor, a betrayer, or an enemy can take away.
And if you have been wounded, the Gospel does not demand that you pretend you were never hurt.
Jesus Himself entered a world of betrayal, humiliation, injustice, and violence.
He was mocked.
He was stripped.
He was falsely accused.
He was crucified.
He knows what it is to suffer at the hands of sinful people.
Yet His suffering was not the end of the story.
On the third day, He rose.
And His resurrection declares that death and evil will not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
This does not mean every painful experience will be neatly resolved in this lifetime.
Some losses remain grievous.
Some consequences endure.
Some justice is still awaited.
But the resurrection gives Christians a hope that is stronger than the grave.
And perhaps someone reading this needs that hope more than another religious slogan.
You do not need someone telling you that your pain was imaginary.
You need to know that Christ is not indifferent to it.
You do not need someone promising that following Jesus will prevent every betrayal.
You need the Savior who remains faithful even when people fail.
You do not need a faith that hides the ugliness of human sin.
You need the Gospel that tells the truth about sin and announces the greater mercy of God.
But there is another person who may need to hear this message.
Not the one who was used.
The one who has used others.
The one who has manipulated people.
The one who has defended cruelty because it was convenient.
The one who has ignored someone's suffering because admitting the truth would require repentance.
The one who has hidden behind religious language while refusing to take responsibility.
The Gospel has a word for you, too.
Repent.
Not merely feel embarrassed.
Not merely regret being exposed.
Turn away from sin.
Tell the truth.
Stop excusing what God calls evil.
Where appropriate and safe, pursue accountability and make restitution.
Do not demand that those you harmed immediately trust you again.
Do not confuse forgiveness with freedom from consequences.
And do not mistake outward religious activity for a transformed heart.
First John 1:9 says:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
There is real forgiveness in Jesus Christ.
But repentance is not a performance designed to escape accountability.
It is a turning of the heart toward God that bears fruit in changed conduct.
And that is where the message of grace becomes so beautiful.
You do not have to defend your old life forever.
You do not have to keep building excuses around the person you have been.
You can come into the light.
You can confess.
You can seek mercy.
You can begin walking in obedience to Christ.
Not because your past was harmless.
But because Jesus Christ is mighty to save.
This is what we mean when we say:
We do not mean that the past never happened.
We do not mean that victims must be silent.
We do not mean that consequences magically disappear.
We mean that sin, shame, suffering, and failure do not have to be the final chapter of a life surrendered to Jesus.
He forgives.
He restores.
He sanctifies.
He teaches us to love what is good and turn away from what destroys.
He creates a people who are called to treat others not as possessions, trophies, or instruments of selfish ambition, but as neighbors made in God's image.
And that brings us back to the window.
To the waiting mother.
To the road.
To the chariots that never arrive.
There is one more detail in Deborah's song that deserves our attention.
Judges 5:31 concludes:
"So let all thine enemies perish, O LORD: but let them that love him be as the sun when he goeth forth in his might."
The song ends with a contrast.
The enemies of the LORD perish.
Those who love Him are compared to the sun rising in strength.
This is the conclusion of the ancient victory hymn, and it should be understood within its own covenantal and historical setting.
It is not permission for Christians to identify anyone who disagrees with them as an enemy to be destroyed.
Jesus explicitly commands His followers to love their enemies and pray for those who persecute them (Matthew 5:44).
The New Testament also teaches that our struggle is not ultimately against flesh and blood (Ephesians 6:12).
We are called to resist evil without becoming cruel ourselves.
To pursue justice without abandoning mercy.
To speak truth without delighting in the humiliation of others.
To remember that the same Christ who calls us to repentance also commands us to love our neighbors.
That includes the vulnerable.
The overlooked.
The wounded.
The person whose story nobody has bothered to hear.
And yes, even the person we find difficult to love.
The Gospel does not make evil acceptable.
It makes a different kind of life possible.
Maybe this is why the Song of Deborah still unsettles us thousands of years later.
Because it exposes the terrible things people can normalize when they believe they are entitled to power.
And because it reminds us that God can overturn what human arrogance considers inevitable.
Sisera had chariots.
He had military strength.
He had the confidence of a conqueror.
His household expected spoils.
But he did not control the outcome.
And the captives his family imagined dividing never became the rewards of that victory.
The LORD had delivered Israel.
Now think about your own life.
What have you allowed to become normal that should have grieved your conscience?
What suffering have you learned to ignore?
What excuses have you made because the truth was uncomfortable?
Where have you mistaken control for strength?
Where have you forgotten that every human being carries dignity that cannot be measured by usefulness, status, appearance, or power?
And where is Jesus calling you to repent?
Not tomorrow.
Not when life becomes easier.
Not when you have found a way to make your sins sound respectable.
Today.
Because there is mercy available in Christ.
And there is no greater freedom than surrendering to the One who died and rose again to save sinners.
Do not let this Scripture remain only something you read and forget.
And think of one person who might need this message.
A friend struggling with shame.
A believer who has confused strength with domination.
Someone who has been wounded by the misuse of power.
Someone who needs to hear that repentance is possible and that grace is not the same thing as pretending evil never happened.
And if you have been strengthened through this ministry, I want to invite you into something deeper.

Our desire is to help people open their Bibles, understand Scripture faithfully, grow in prayer, confront sin honestly, receive the comfort of the Gospel, and become more deeply rooted in Jesus Christ.
We want those resources to continue reaching people who need them.
We want biblical encouragement to travel farther.
We want wounded believers to find nourishment, struggling disciples to find sound teaching, and curious seekers to encounter the truth of Jesus Christ.
And we want to keep building resources that help people move beyond momentary inspiration into lasting spiritual growth.
That work requires time, care, and practical support.
Scripture teaches in 2 Corinthians 9:7 that giving should be purposeful, willing, and cheerful—not compelled.
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not through guilt.
Not through fear.
Not through a promise that financial support will purchase God's favor.
But through a shared desire to serve Christ and make His Word more accessible.
The greater purpose is that more people would come to know Jesus, understand His Word, and grow as His disciples.
Pray for this ministry.
Use the free resources.
Speak about Jesus with compassion and courage.
It is about the glory of God and the salvation and transformation of people through Jesus Christ.
And that is why this ancient song matters so much.
The enemy expected to count women among the spoils.
But Deborah's song remembers the defeat of the oppressor.
The world expected the strong to take whatever they wanted.
But the God of Israel heard the cries of His people.
And centuries later, the Son of God entered our broken world, not to exploit the helpless, but to give Himself for sinners.
The cross does not tell us that human cruelty is insignificant.
It tells us that sin is serious enough to require redemption and that God's love is great enough to provide a Savior.
So when you close this article, remember the woman at the window.
Remember the captives her household expected.
Remember the LORD who delivered the oppressed.
And above all, remember Jesus Christ.
The crucified and risen King.
The Savior who calls sinners to repentance.
The Lord who teaches His people to love.
The Redeemer whose grace can change the direction of a human life.
Because the world may remember what was done to you, and your conscience may remember what you have done—but in Jesus Christ, neither wound nor sin has to write your final chapter.
